items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "magnification"?
options: A microscope slide with a scale of known divisions (often 0.01 mm = 10 μm each) used to calibrate an eyepiece graticule.
The number of times larger an image is than the real size of the object (image size ÷ actual size).
A transparent scale in the eyepiece of a light microscope, with arbitrary divisions that must be calibrated for each objective lens.
The ability to distinguish between two separate points; the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as separate.
items.answer: The number of times larger an image is than the real size of the object (image size ÷ actual size).
items.markingKey: Magnification: the number of times larger an image is than the real size of the object (image size ÷ actual size).

items.stem: Explain the difference between magnification and resolution.
items.answer: Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the object; resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points as separate. Increasing magnification beyond the resolution limit gives no more detail.
items.markingKey: magnification defined [1]; resolution defined [1]; more magnification gives no more detail beyond the resolution limit [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why living cells cannot be viewed with a transmission electron microscope.
items.answer: The specimen must be in a vacuum (electrons are scattered by air) and must be very thin, dehydrated and stained with heavy metals, which kills the cells.
items.markingKey: vacuum [1]; preparation (thin sections / dehydration / heavy-metal stains) kills cells [1] [2]

items.stem: A micrograph of a Golgi vesicle has a scale bar labelled 50 nm. The scale bar is 10 mm long and the image of a Golgi vesicle is 17 mm long. (a) Use the scale bar to calculate the magnification. (b) Calculate the actual length of a Golgi vesicle.
The actual length of a chloroplast is 8.00 μm. In a photomicrograph produced by Hana, the image of a chloroplast is 20 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph. Show your working.

A micrograph of a lymphocyte has a scale bar labelled 10 μm. The scale bar is 40 mm long and the image of a lymphocyte is 39 mm long. (a) Use the scale bar to calculate the magnification. (b) Calculate the actual length of a lymphocyte.

Kenji in Accra measures five examples of a xylem vessel element (width) using an eyepiece graticule. At the magnification used, 50 graticule divisions equal 20 divisions of a stage micrometer (1 division = 10 μm). The lengths in graticule divisions were 23, 20, 29, 27, 23. (a) Calculate the mean actual length of the cells in μm. (b) Suggest why the cells could not be measured accurately using the scale on a ruler held against the eyepiece.
items.answer: (a) 97.6 μm (b) The ruler is not in the optical path; its scale is not superimposed on the image and is not calibrated against a known length.
items.markingKey: (a) one division = 200 ÷ 50 = 4 μm [1]; mean divisions = 24.4 [1]; × 4 = 97.6 μm [1] [3] (b) The ruler is not in the optical path; its scale is not superimposed on the image and is not calibrated against a known length [1]

items.stem: Elena in Jakarta measures five examples of a cheek epithelial cell using an eyepiece graticule. At the magnification used, 80 graticule divisions equal 80 divisions of a stage micrometer (1 division = 10 μm). The lengths in graticule divisions were 4, 4, 6, 6, 7. (a) Explain why five cells were measured rather than one. (b) Suggest why the cells could not be measured accurately using the scale on a ruler held against the eyepiece. (c) Explain why these cells could be studied with a light microscope but their ribosomes could not.
items.answer: (a) Cells vary in size; a mean of several gives a more representative / reliable value. (b) The ruler is not in the optical path; its scale is not superimposed on the image and is not calibrated against a known length. (c) The cells are larger than the resolution of a light microscope (about 200 nm); ribosomes (about 25 nm) are smaller than this, so need an electron microscope.
items.markingKey: (a) variation between cells [1]; mean more representative [1] [2] (b) The ruler is not in the optical path; its scale is not superimposed on the image and is not calibrated against a known length [1] (c) resolution limit 200 nm [1]; ribosomes smaller [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the approximate maximum resolution of a light microscope?
items.answer: 200 nm
items.markingKey: Limited by the wavelength of light (about 400–700 nm): about 200 nm (0.2 μm).

items.stem: Describe how an eyepiece graticule is calibrated using a stage micrometer.
items.answer: Place the stage micrometer on the stage and line up its scale with the graticule scale; count how many stage micrometer divisions match a number of graticule divisions; calculate the length of one graticule division (e.g. in μm); repeat for each objective lens.
items.markingKey: line up scales [1]; count matching divisions [1]; calculate value of one division [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a scanning electron micrograph shows the surface of a cell but not its organelles.
items.answer: In SEM the electron beam is reflected (scattered) from the surface rather than passing through the specimen, so it gives a 3-D image of the surface only.
items.markingKey: electrons reflected from surface [1]; no internal detail / 3-D surface image [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why images from an electron microscope are in black and white, though they are often coloured afterwards.
items.answer: Electrons are not visible light and have no colour; the image is formed on a screen from electrons hitting it, so false colour is added by computer.
items.markingKey: electrons have no colour / not visible light [1]; false colour added [1] [2]

items.stem: The actual length of a chloroplast is 5.70 μm. In a photomicrograph produced by Diego, the image of a chloroplast is 114 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph. Show your working.
Grace measures the image of a lysosome in a micrograph as 26 mm. The magnification is ×40,000. Calculate the actual length of a lysosome, giving your answer in nanometres (nm).
items.answer: 650 nm

items.stem: Compare light microscopes and electron microscopes, with reference to magnification, resolution and the specimens that can be viewed.
items.answer: LM: light (wavelength 400–700 nm), resolution about 200 nm, magnification up to ×1500, living or dead specimens, colour stains, cheap. EM: electrons (short wavelength), resolution about 0.5 nm, magnification up to ×500 000, vacuum so dead specimens, heavy-metal stains, black and white images, TEM sections vs SEM surfaces, expensive.
items.markingKey: resolution values [2]; reason (wavelength) [1]; magnification values [1]; specimens living / dead and preparation [1]; TEM vs SEM [1] [6]

items.stem: Describe how you would use a light microscope, eyepiece graticule and stage micrometer to determine the mean diameter of cells in a prepared slide.
items.answer: Calibrate graticule: line up with stage micrometer, find value of one division for the objective; replace with specimen slide; measure diameter of each cell in graticule divisions; measure at least 5–10 cells chosen at random; convert to μm; calculate mean.
items.markingKey: calibration steps [2]; same objective [1]; measure several cells / random [1]; convert divisions to μm [1]; mean [1] [6]

items.stem: What is the name for "site of aerobic respiration (Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation) producing ATP"?
items.answer: Mitochondrion
items.markingKey: Mitochondrion: site of aerobic respiration (Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation) producing ATP.

items.stem: Explain how the RER and Golgi body work together to produce glycoproteins for secretion.
items.answer: Polypeptides made by ribosomes on RER enter the cisternae and are folded; vesicles carry them to the Golgi body, which adds carbohydrate and modifies them; they are packaged into secretory vesicles that fuse with the cell surface membrane.
items.markingKey: protein made on RER [1]; vesicles to Golgi [1]; carbohydrate added / modified [1]; secretory vesicles / exocytosis [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why ATP is described as the universal energy currency.
items.answer: ATP is used in all cells as the immediate source of energy for processes such as active transport and protein synthesis; it is made in respiration and hydrolysed to ADP + Pi, releasing energy in small, manageable amounts.
items.markingKey: used by all cells / all processes [1]; hydrolysis releases energy in small amounts [1] [2]

items.stem: Suggest which organelles would be present in large numbers in a plasma cell producing antibodies, and explain why.
items.answer: Rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body: antibodies are glycoproteins made on the RER and modified and packaged by the Golgi body.
items.markingKey: rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body [1]; antibodies are glycoproteins made on the RER and modified and packaged by the Golgi body [1] [2]

items.stem: Suggest and explain which organelles would be particularly numerous in (i) a pancreatic acinar cell secreting digestive enzymes (ii) a heart muscle cell.
items.answer: (i) Rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body: large amounts of protein are made on the RER and packaged into secretory vesicles by the Golgi body. (ii) Mitochondria: continuous contraction requires a large supply of ATP from aerobic respiration.
items.markingKey: (i) rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body [1]; reason [1] (ii) mitochondria [1]; reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Suggest and explain which organelles would be particularly numerous in (i) a palisade mesophyll cell (ii) a cell in the adrenal cortex secreting steroid hormones.
items.answer: (i) Chloroplasts: chloroplasts absorb light for photosynthesis. (ii) Smooth endoplasmic reticulum: steroid hormones are lipids synthesised by the SER.
items.markingKey: (i) chloroplasts [1]; reason [1] (ii) smooth endoplasmic reticulum [1]; reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Researchers in Kuala Lumpur supplied a goblet cell with radioactively labelled amino acids for 3 minutes and then tracked the radioactivity as the cell made and secreted mucin (a glycoprotein). (a) Explain why the radioactivity first appears in the rough endoplasmic reticulum. (b) Explain why the cell would also contain a large nucleolus.
items.answer: (a) Amino acids are joined into polypeptides by ribosomes attached to the RER, and the polypeptide enters the RER lumen. (b) The nucleolus makes ribosomes; many ribosomes are needed for the high rate of protein synthesis.
items.markingKey: (a) Amino acids are joined into polypeptides by ribosomes attached to the RER [1]; and the polypeptide enters the RER lumen [1] [2] (b) The nucleolus makes ribosomes [1]; many ribosomes are needed for the high rate of protein synthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: Researchers in Manila supplied a plasma cell with radioactively labelled amino acids for 3 minutes and then tracked the radioactivity as the cell made and secreted antibodies. (a) State, in order, the organelles in which the radioactivity would appear. (b) Explain why the cell would also contain a large nucleolus.
items.answer: (a) Ribosomes on RER → RER cisternae → transport vesicles → Golgi body → secretory vesicles → (outside cell). (b) The nucleolus makes ribosomes; many ribosomes are needed for the high rate of protein synthesis.
items.markingKey: (a) RER [1]; Golgi [1]; secretory vesicles [1] [3] (b) The nucleolus makes ribosomes [1]; many ribosomes are needed for the high rate of protein synthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: An electron micrograph shows an organelle with this structure: "double membrane, internal membranes (thylakoids) stacked into grana, stroma containing starch grains, 70S ribosomes and circular DNA".
items.answer: Chloroplast
items.markingKey: Chloroplast: double membrane, internal membranes (thylakoids) stacked into grana, stroma containing starch grains, 70S ribosomes and circular DNA.

items.stem: Explain the role of the nuclear pores.
items.answer: They allow large molecules such as mRNA and ribosomal subunits to leave the nucleus and molecules such as nucleotides and enzymes to enter.
items.markingKey: mRNA / ribosomes out [1]; substances in [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why lysosomes are important in cells such as phagocytes.
items.answer: Lysosomes fuse with phagocytic vesicles containing bacteria and release hydrolytic enzymes that digest them.
items.markingKey: fuse with phagocytic vesicle [1]; hydrolytic enzymes digest [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the role of centrioles in an animal cell.
items.answer: Centrioles in the centrosome organise microtubules to form the spindle that separates chromosomes during nuclear division; they also form basal bodies of cilia.
items.markingKey: spindle / microtubule organising [1]; separating chromosomes in division [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists in Dhaka estimated the percentage of cell volume occupied by mitochondria in three cell types: sperm midpiece 46.9%; skin epidermal cell 6.9%; fat storage cell 3.0%. Calculate how many times greater the percentage is in the sperm midpiece than in the cell type with the lowest value.

Scientists in Kuala Lumpur estimated the percentage of cell volume occupied by mitochondria in three cell types: fat storage cell 3.0%; skin epidermal cell 5.1%; pancreatic acinar cell 7.4%. (a) Suggest why the pancreatic acinar cell has the highest proportion of mitochondria. (b) Explain why mitochondria cannot be seen in detail with a light microscope.
items.answer: (a) It has a high demand for ATP (e.g. contraction / movement / active processes), supplied by aerobic respiration in mitochondria. (b) They are only about 1 μm wide, close to the resolution limit of a light microscope (about 0.2 μm), so internal cristae cannot be resolved.
items.markingKey: (a) high ATP demand linked to function [1]; aerobic respiration in mitochondria [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: They are only about 1 μm wide; close to the resolution limit of a light microscope (about 0.2 μm); so internal cristae cannot be resolved (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Researchers in Cairo supplied a goblet cell with radioactively labelled amino acids for 20 minutes and then tracked the radioactivity as the cell made and secreted mucin (a glycoprotein). (a) Explain why the radioactivity first appears in the rough endoplasmic reticulum. (b) Suggest why this cell contains many mitochondria. (c) Explain why the cell would also contain a large nucleolus.
items.answer: (a) Amino acids are joined into polypeptides by ribosomes attached to the RER, and the polypeptide enters the RER lumen. (b) To provide ATP for protein synthesis, vesicle movement and exocytosis. (c) The nucleolus makes ribosomes; many ribosomes are needed for the high rate of protein synthesis.
items.markingKey: (a) Amino acids are joined into polypeptides by ribosomes attached to the RER [1]; and the polypeptide enters the RER lumen [1] [2] (b) To provide ATP for protein synthesis [1]; vesicle movement and exocytosis [1] [2] (c) The nucleolus makes ribosomes [1]; many ribosomes are needed for the high rate of protein synthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the name for "an organism whose cells have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, such as a bacterium"?
items.answer: Prokaryote
items.markingKey: Prokaryote: an organism whose cells have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, such as a bacterium.

items.stem: Explain why antibiotics that target 70S ribosomes can be used to treat bacterial infections in humans.
items.answer: Bacteria have 70S ribosomes but human cytoplasm has 80S ribosomes, so bacterial protein synthesis is inhibited without harming human cells (mostly).
items.markingKey: 70S vs 80S [1]; selective inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: Compare the genetic material of a prokaryote with that of a eukaryote.
items.answer: Prokaryote: circular DNA free in cytoplasm (nucleoid), no histones, plasmids may be present. Eukaryote: linear DNA in chromosomes in a nucleus, associated with histones.
items.markingKey: circular vs linear [1]; no nucleus vs nucleus [1]; histones [1] [3]

items.stem: A scientist in Accra examines a cell grown from a throat swab with an electron microscope and records: a nucleus with a nuclear envelope; 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm; cytoplasm. State whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic and give two reasons from the observations.
items.answer: Eukaryotic: a nucleus with a nuclear envelope; 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
items.markingKey: eukaryotic [1]; two correct reasons from the observations (not the shared feature) [2] [3]

items.stem: A scientist in Bogotá examines a cell isolated from a hot spring with an electron microscope and records: a diameter of about 2 μm; plasmids; cytoplasm. State whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic and give two reasons from the observations.
items.answer: Prokaryotic: a diameter of about 2 μm; plasmids.
items.markingKey: prokaryotic [1]; two correct reasons from the observations (not the shared feature) [2] [3]

items.stem: A transmission electron micrograph of Vibrio cholerae at ×15,000 shows a cell wall, a capsule, a circular DNA molecule, plasmids, 70S ribosomes and a flagellum. The cell is 18 mm long in the micrograph. (a) Calculate the actual length of the cell in μm. (b) Suggest why the presence of plasmids may make infections with this bacterium more difficult to treat.
items.answer: (a) 1.2 μm (b) Plasmids may carry antibiotic-resistance genes that can be transferred to other bacteria.
items.markingKey: (a) 18 mm = 18000 μm; ÷ 15,000 = 1.2 μm [2] (b) Plasmids may carry antibiotic-resistance genes that can be transferred to other bacteria [2] [2]

items.stem: Explain why bacteria cannot carry out the modification of proteins in the same way as eukaryotic cells.
items.answer: They lack membrane-bound organelles such as the RER and Golgi body, which modify and package proteins (e.g. adding carbohydrate).
items.markingKey: no RER / Golgi [1]; these modify proteins [1] [2]

items.stem: Mateo says: "Bacterial cell walls are made of cellulose, like plant cells." Explain whether Mateo is correct.
items.answer: Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan (murein).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan (murein). [2]

items.stem: A spherical bacterium (coccus) has a diameter of 1.3 μm and a spherical eukaryotic cell has a diameter of 80 μm. (a) Calculate how many times larger the diameter of the eukaryotic cell is. (b) Using V = 4/3 πr³, calculate how many times larger its volume is.
items.markingKey: (a) 80 ÷ 1.3 = 61.5 [1] (b) volumes 268,000 μm³ and 1.15 μm³ [1]; ratio 233,000 (= ratio of diameters cubed) [1] [3]

items.stem: A spherical bacterium (coccus) has a diameter of 1.7 μm and a spherical eukaryotic cell has a diameter of 10 μm. (a) Calculate how many times larger the diameter of the eukaryotic cell is. (b) Using V = 4/3 πr³, calculate how many times larger its volume is. (c) Explain why prokaryotic cells do not need specialised transport systems inside the cell.
items.answer: (a) 5.9 (b) 204 (c) Their small size gives a large surface area to volume ratio and short diffusion distances, so diffusion is fast enough.
items.markingKey: (a) 10 ÷ 1.7 = 5.9 [1] (b) volumes 524 μm³ and 2.57 μm³ [1]; ratio 204 (= ratio of diameters cubed) [1] (c) large SA:V [1]; short diffusion distance [1] [5]

items.stem: A scientist in Santiago examines a cell found in a soil sample with an electron microscope and records: DNA associated with histone proteins in linear chromosomes; mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum; ribosomes. State whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic and give two reasons from the observations.
items.answer: Eukaryotic: DNA associated with histone proteins in linear chromosomes; mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum.
items.markingKey: eukaryotic [1]; two correct reasons from the observations (not the shared feature) [2] [3]

items.stem: Which term is defined as "one of the protein subunits that make up a viral capsid"?
items.answer: Capsomere
items.markingKey: Capsomere: one of the protein subunits that make up a viral capsid.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "a virus that infects bacteria"?
items.answer: Bacteriophage
items.markingKey: Bacteriophage: a virus that infects bacteria.

items.stem: Explain why viruses are described as obligate parasites.
items.answer: They have no metabolism or ribosomes of their own, so they can only reproduce inside a host cell using its enzymes, ribosomes and ATP.
items.markingKey: no metabolism / ribosomes [1]; must use host cell to reproduce [1] [2]

items.stem: A micrograph of a measles virus has a scale bar labelled 100 nm. The scale bar is 20 mm long and the image of a measles virus is 32 mm long. (a) Use the scale bar to calculate the magnification. (b) Calculate the actual length of a measles virus.

A student in Cape Town reads that HIV contains RNA, has a diameter of about 200 nm and infects T helper lymphocytes. (a) Calculate the diameter of the virus in μm. (b) Explain why HIV infects only T helper lymphocytes.
items.answer: (a) 0.2 μm (b) Proteins / glycoproteins on the virus surface are complementary to specific receptors found only on the surface of those cells.
items.markingKey: (a) 200 ÷ 1000 = 0.2 μm [1] (b) Proteins / glycoproteins on the virus surface are complementary to specific receptors found only on the surface of those cells [2] [2]

items.stem: Why are viruses described as non-cellular?
options: They contain RNA instead of DNA
They have no cytoplasm, ribosomes or cell membrane of their own
items.answer: They have no cytoplasm, ribosomes or cell membrane of their own
items.markingKey: Viruses have only nucleic acid and a protein coat (sometimes an envelope); they cannot metabolise.

items.stem: A micrograph of an influenza virus has a scale bar labelled 200 nm. The scale bar is 40 mm long and the image of an influenza virus is 19 mm long. (a) Use the scale bar to calculate the magnification. (b) Calculate the actual length of an influenza virus.

A student in Bogotá reads that a bacteriophage contains DNA, has a diameter of about 30 nm and infects bacteria. (a) Calculate the diameter of the virus in μm. (b) Describe the structure of a typical virus particle.
items.answer: (a) 0.03 μm (b) Nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein capsid made of capsomeres; some have a phospholipid envelope with glycoproteins.
items.markingKey: (a) 30 ÷ 1000 = 0.03 μm [1] (b) Nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein capsid made of capsomeres [2]; some have a phospholipid envelope with glycoproteins [1] [3]

items.stem: Why does an electron microscope have a higher resolution than a light microscope?
options: Electron beams have a much shorter wavelength than light
Electrons can be focused with glass lenses
items.answer: Electron beams have a much shorter wavelength than light
items.markingKey: Resolution depends on wavelength; electrons have a much shorter wavelength.

items.stem: Ines says: "One division on an eyepiece graticule is always 10 μm." Explain whether Ines is correct.
items.answer: Graticule divisions are arbitrary; their value depends on the objective lens and must be calibrated with a stage micrometer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Graticule divisions are arbitrary; their value depends on the objective lens and must be calibrated with a stage micrometer. [2]

items.stem: A student in Dhaka states: "An electron microscope has a higher resolution because it has a higher magnification." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Its higher resolution is due to the shorter wavelength of electrons; magnification alone does not increase resolution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Its higher resolution is due to the shorter wavelength of electrons; magnification alone does not increase resolution. [2]

items.stem: Nadia calibrates an eyepiece graticule using a stage micrometer with divisions of 0.01 mm. With the ×20 objective, 80 eyepiece graticule divisions line up exactly with 40 stage micrometer divisions. (a) Calculate the length of one eyepiece graticule division in μm. (b) A root tip meristem cell measures 4 eyepiece divisions. Calculate its actual length.
items.answer: (a) 5 μm (b) 20 μm

items.stem: A micrograph of a microvillus has a scale bar labelled 2 μm. The scale bar is 30 mm long and the image of a microvillus is 16 mm long. (a) Use the scale bar to calculate the magnification. (b) Calculate the actual length of a microvillus.

Felix in Lisbon measures five examples of a lymphocyte using an eyepiece graticule. At the magnification used, 80 graticule divisions equal 10 divisions of a stage micrometer (1 division = 10 μm). The lengths in graticule divisions were 9, 7, 8, 7, 8. (a) State one source of error when measuring with an eyepiece graticule and suggest how to reduce it. (b) Explain why these cells could be studied with a light microscope but their ribosomes could not.
items.answer: (a) Cell edges may not line up with divisions / estimating part divisions; use a higher magnification or measure more cells. (b) The cells are larger than the resolution of a light microscope (about 200 nm); ribosomes (about 25 nm) are smaller than this, so need an electron microscope.
items.markingKey: (a) error [1]; improvement [1] [2] (b) resolution limit 200 nm [1]; ribosomes smaller [1] [2]

items.stem: Which structure is found in some animal cells but not in typical plant cells?
items.answer: Centriole
items.markingKey: Centriole occur in animal cells only.

items.stem: A student in Bogotá states: "Ribosomes are surrounded by a single membrane." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Ribosomes are not membrane-bound; they are made of rRNA and protein.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Ribosomes are not membrane-bound; they are made of rRNA and protein. [2]

items.stem: Priya writes in a revision note: "Plant cells do not have mitochondria because they have chloroplasts." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Plant cells have both mitochondria and chloroplasts; they respire all the time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Plant cells have both mitochondria and chloroplasts; they respire all the time. [2]

items.stem: Scientists in Santiago estimated the percentage of cell volume occupied by mitochondria in three cell types: pancreatic acinar cell 8.3%; heart muscle cell 39.5%; sperm midpiece 39.5%. A pancreatic acinar cell has a volume of 4000 μm³. Calculate the volume occupied by its mitochondria.
items.answer: 332 μm³

items.stem: Suggest and explain which organelles would be particularly numerous in (i) a plasma cell producing antibodies (ii) a root hair cell absorbing mineral ions.
items.answer: (i) Rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body: antibodies are glycoproteins made on the RER and modified and packaged by the Golgi body. (ii) Mitochondria: active transport of ions against their concentration gradient needs ATP.
items.markingKey: (i) rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi body [1]; reason [1] (ii) mitochondria [1]; reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Describe the structure of a typical plant cell as seen with an electron microscope and compare it with a typical animal cell.
items.answer: Both: nucleus with envelope and pores, nucleolus, RER, SER, Golgi, mitochondria, 80S ribosomes, cell surface membrane. Plant only: cellulose cell wall, plasmodesmata, chloroplasts with grana, large permanent vacuole with tonoplast. Animal only: centrioles, sometimes microvilli and cilia; small temporary vacuoles; glycogen rather than starch.
items.markingKey: four shared structures [2]; plant-only features [2]; animal-only features [1]; storage carbohydrate / vacuole contrast [1] [6]

items.stem: What is the name for "an organism whose cells have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, such as a bacterium"?
items.answer: Prokaryote
items.markingKey: Prokaryote: an organism whose cells have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, such as a bacterium.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Compare the genetic material of a prokaryote with that of a eukaryote. (b) Explain why antibiotics that target 70S ribosomes can be used to treat bacterial infections in humans.
items.answer: (a) Prokaryote: circular DNA free in cytoplasm (nucleoid), no histones, plasmids may be present. Eukaryote: linear DNA in chromosomes in a nucleus, associated with histones. (b) Bacteria have 70S ribosomes but human cytoplasm has 80S ribosomes, so bacterial protein synthesis is inhibited without harming human cells (mostly).
items.markingKey: (a) circular vs linear [1]; no nucleus vs nucleus [1]; histones [1] [3] (b) 70S vs 80S [1]; selective inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: A scientist in Santiago examines a cell found in a soil sample with an electron microscope and records: cell wall made of peptidoglycan (murein); a diameter of about 2 μm; a cell surface membrane. State whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic and give two reasons from the observations.
items.answer: Prokaryotic: cell wall made of peptidoglycan (murein); a diameter of about 2 μm.
items.markingKey: prokaryotic [1]; two correct reasons from the observations (not the shared feature) [2] [3]

items.stem: Compare the structure of a prokaryotic cell with that of a eukaryotic animal cell.
items.answer: Prokaryote: 0.5–5 μm, no nucleus, circular DNA without histones, plasmids, 70S ribosomes, peptidoglycan wall, sometimes capsule / pili / flagellum, no membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryote: 10–100 μm, nucleus with envelope, linear chromosomes with histones, 80S ribosomes, no wall, membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes). Both: cell surface membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA.
items.markingKey: similarities [1]; size [1]; nucleus / DNA form [1]; ribosomes [1]; wall [1]; organelles [1] [6]

items.stem: A transmission electron micrograph of Staphylococcus aureus at ×20,000 shows a cell wall, a capsule, a circular DNA molecule, plasmids, 70S ribosomes and a flagellum. The cell is 44 mm long in the micrograph. (a) List three ways in which this cell differs from a cell from the human lining of the trachea. (b) State the function of the capsule. (c) Suggest why the presence of plasmids may make infections with this bacterium more difficult to treat.
items.answer: (a) No nucleus (DNA free / circular); peptidoglycan wall; capsule; 70S not 80S ribosomes; plasmids; no membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic flagellum not cilia. (b) Protects the bacterium (from phagocytosis / drying out) and helps it stick to surfaces. (c) Plasmids may carry antibiotic-resistance genes that can be transferred to other bacteria.
items.markingKey: (a) any 3 from: No nucleus (DNA free / circular); peptidoglycan wall; capsule; 70S not 80S ribosomes; plasmids; no membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic flagellum not cilia (1 mark each) [3] (b) Protects the bacterium (from phagocytosis / drying out) and helps it stick to surfaces [1] (c) Plasmids may carry antibiotic-resistance genes that can be transferred to other bacteria [2] [2]

items.stem: Explain why antibiotics are not effective against viruses.
items.answer: Antibiotics target bacterial structures or processes (cell walls, 70S ribosomes) that viruses do not have; viruses reproduce inside host cells.
items.markingKey: no cell wall / ribosomes / metabolism [1]; inside host cells [1] [2]

items.stem: The actual length of a tobacco mosaic virus particle is 300 nm. In a photomicrograph produced by Daniel, the image of a tobacco mosaic virus particle is 15 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the photomicrograph. Show your working.

A micrograph of a measles virus has a scale bar labelled 100 nm. The scale bar is 15 mm long and the image of a measles virus is 18 mm long. (a) Use the scale bar to calculate the magnification. (b) Calculate the actual length of a measles virus.
Which structure can be seen with an electron microscope but not with a light microscope?
items.answer: A ribosome
items.markingKey: Ribosomes (about 20–25 nm) are below the resolution of a light microscope.

items.stem: Tomás writes in a revision note: "One division on an eyepiece graticule is always 10 μm." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Graticule divisions are arbitrary; their value depends on the objective lens and must be calibrated with a stage micrometer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Graticule divisions are arbitrary; their value depends on the objective lens and must be calibrated with a stage micrometer. [2]

items.stem: Yusuf writes in a revision note: "An electron microscope has a higher resolution because it has a higher magnification." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Its higher resolution is due to the shorter wavelength of electrons; magnification alone does not increase resolution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Its higher resolution is due to the shorter wavelength of electrons; magnification alone does not increase resolution. [2]

items.stem: Omar calibrates an eyepiece graticule using a stage micrometer with divisions of 0.01 mm. With the ×20 objective, 100 eyepiece graticule divisions line up exactly with 50 stage micrometer divisions. (a) Calculate the length of one eyepiece graticule division in μm. (b) A pollen grain measures 8 eyepiece divisions. Calculate its actual length.
items.answer: (a) 5 μm (b) 40 μm

items.stem: A micrograph of a pollen grain has a scale bar labelled 5 μm. The scale bar is 10 mm long and the image of a pollen grain is 48 mm long. (a) Use the scale bar to calculate the magnification. (b) Calculate the actual length of a pollen grain.

Aisha in Muscat measures five examples of a Paramecium using an eyepiece graticule. At the magnification used, 50 graticule divisions equal 50 divisions of a stage micrometer (1 division = 10 μm). The lengths in graticule divisions were 24, 22, 19, 19, 14. (a) Explain why these cells could be studied with a light microscope but their ribosomes could not. (b) Compare the preparation of a specimen for a light microscope with preparation for a transmission electron microscope.
items.answer: (a) The cells are larger than the resolution of a light microscope (about 200 nm); ribosomes (about 25 nm) are smaller than this, so need an electron microscope. (b) LM: thin section or smear, water mount, coloured stains, can be living. TEM: very thin section, dehydrated, heavy-metal stains, in vacuum, must be dead.
items.markingKey: (a) resolution limit 200 nm [1]; ribosomes smaller [1] [2] (b) two valid comparisons [2]

items.stem: Which sequence shows the route taken by an extracellular protein from its site of synthesis to secretion?
options: Smooth ER → lysosome → Golgi body → vesicle → cell surface membrane
Golgi body → RER → vesicle → lysosome → cell surface membrane
Ribosome in cytoplasm → nucleus → Golgi body → cell surface membrane
Ribosome on RER → RER → vesicle → Golgi body → vesicle → cell surface membrane
items.answer: Ribosome on RER → RER → vesicle → Golgi body → vesicle → cell surface membrane
items.markingKey: Protein made on ribosomes of RER, transported in vesicles to the Golgi body, modified and packaged into secretory vesicles which fuse with the cell surface membrane (exocytosis).

items.stem: Zara says: "The Golgi body makes proteins." Explain whether Zara is correct.
items.answer: Proteins are made by ribosomes (often on RER); the Golgi body modifies and packages them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Proteins are made by ribosomes (often on RER); the Golgi body modifies and packages them. [2]

items.stem: Mateo says: "Plant cells do not have mitochondria because they have chloroplasts." Explain whether Mateo is correct.
items.answer: Plant cells have both mitochondria and chloroplasts; they respire all the time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Plant cells have both mitochondria and chloroplasts; they respire all the time. [2]

items.stem: Suggest which organelles would be present in large numbers in a liver cell detoxifying drugs and making cholesterol, and explain why.
items.answer: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum: lipids and steroids are made and toxins are broken down in the SER.
items.markingKey: smooth endoplasmic reticulum [1]; lipids and steroids are made and toxins are broken down in the SER [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists in Mumbai estimated the percentage of cell volume occupied by mitochondria in three cell types: sperm midpiece 39.5%; fat storage cell 2.9%; pancreatic acinar cell 8.3%. (a) Calculate how many times greater the percentage is in the sperm midpiece than in the cell type with the lowest value. (b) Explain why mitochondria cannot be seen in detail with a light microscope.
items.answer: (a) 13.6 (b) They are only about 1 μm wide, close to the resolution limit of a light microscope (about 0.2 μm), so internal cristae cannot be resolved.
items.markingKey: (a) 39.5 ÷ 2.9 = 13.6 [2] (b) any 2 from: They are only about 1 μm wide; close to the resolution limit of a light microscope (about 0.2 μm); so internal cristae cannot be resolved (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Researchers in Nairobi supplied a β cell in the islets of Langerhans with radioactively labelled amino acids for 5 minutes and then tracked the radioactivity as the cell made and secreted insulin. (a) Explain why the radioactivity first appears in the rough endoplasmic reticulum. (b) Describe how insulin leaves the cell. (c) Suggest why this cell contains many mitochondria.
items.answer: (a) Amino acids are joined into polypeptides by ribosomes attached to the RER, and the polypeptide enters the RER lumen. (b) By exocytosis: secretory vesicles move to and fuse with the cell surface membrane, releasing the contents; this requires ATP. (c) To provide ATP for protein synthesis, vesicle movement and exocytosis.
items.markingKey: (a) Amino acids are joined into polypeptides by ribosomes attached to the RER [1]; and the polypeptide enters the RER lumen [1] [2] (b) vesicles fuse with membrane [1]; exocytosis / ATP [1] [2] (c) To provide ATP for protein synthesis [1]; vesicle movement and exocytosis [1] [2]

items.stem: Which feature is found in prokaryotic cells but not in eukaryotic cells?
options: DNA associated with histone proteins in linear chromosomes
items.answer: No membrane-bound organelles
items.markingKey: No membrane-bound organelles is a prokaryotic feature.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Compare the genetic material of a prokaryote with that of a eukaryote. (b) Explain why antibiotics that target 70S ribosomes can be used to treat bacterial infections in humans.
items.answer: (a) Prokaryote: circular DNA free in cytoplasm (nucleoid), no histones, plasmids may be present. Eukaryote: linear DNA in chromosomes in a nucleus, associated with histones. (b) Bacteria have 70S ribosomes but human cytoplasm has 80S ribosomes, so bacterial protein synthesis is inhibited without harming human cells (mostly).
items.markingKey: (a) circular vs linear [1]; no nucleus vs nucleus [1]; histones [1] [3] (b) 70S vs 80S [1]; selective inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: A scientist in Santiago examines a cell grown from a throat swab with an electron microscope and records: a nucleus with a nuclear envelope; mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum; cytoplasm. State whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic and give two reasons from the observations.
items.answer: Eukaryotic: a nucleus with a nuclear envelope; mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum.
items.markingKey: eukaryotic [1]; two correct reasons from the observations (not the shared feature) [2] [3]

items.stem: A transmission electron micrograph of Escherichia coli at ×25,000 shows a cell wall, a capsule, a circular DNA molecule, plasmids, 70S ribosomes and a flagellum. The cell is 75 mm long in the micrograph. (a) Calculate the actual length of the cell in μm. (b) Explain why the bacterium is classified as a prokaryote. (c) Suggest why the presence of plasmids may make infections with this bacterium more difficult to treat.
items.answer: (a) 3 μm (b) It has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm. (c) Plasmids may carry antibiotic-resistance genes that can be transferred to other bacteria.
items.markingKey: (a) 75 mm = 75000 μm; ÷ 25,000 = 3 μm [2] (b) It has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles [1]; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm [1] [2] (c) Plasmids may carry antibiotic-resistance genes that can be transferred to other bacteria [2] [2]

items.stem: A transmission electron micrograph of Staphylococcus aureus at ×15,000 shows a cell wall, a capsule, a circular DNA molecule, plasmids, 70S ribosomes and a flagellum. The cell is 43.5 mm long in the micrograph. (a) List three ways in which this cell differs from a cell from the human lining of the trachea. (b) State the function of the capsule. (c) Explain why the bacterium is classified as a prokaryote.
items.answer: (a) No nucleus (DNA free / circular); peptidoglycan wall; capsule; 70S not 80S ribosomes; plasmids; no membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic flagellum not cilia. (b) Protects the bacterium (from phagocytosis / drying out) and helps it stick to surfaces. (c) It has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm.
items.markingKey: (a) any 3 from: No nucleus (DNA free / circular); peptidoglycan wall; capsule; 70S not 80S ribosomes; plasmids; no membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic flagellum not cilia (1 mark each) [3] (b) Protects the bacterium (from phagocytosis / drying out) and helps it stick to surfaces [1] (c) It has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles [1]; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the envelope of HIV helps it infect host cells.
items.answer: The envelope contains glycoproteins that bind to CD4 receptors on T helper cells; the envelope fuses with the cell surface membrane so the capsid enters the cell.
items.markingKey: glycoproteins bind receptors [1]; fusion with membrane [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas measures the image of a bacteriophage T4 in a micrograph as 32 mm. The magnification is ×150,000. Calculate the actual length of a bacteriophage T4, giving your answer in nanometres (nm).
items.answer: 213 nm

items.stem: A micrograph of an influenza virus has a scale bar labelled 50 nm. The scale bar is 10 mm long and the image of an influenza virus is 18 mm long. (a) Use the scale bar to calculate the magnification. (b) Calculate the actual length of an influenza virus.
